blocks.text: Planning a trip around Greece often starts with a simple list: Athens, Santorini, Mykonos. Then you look at the map, add another island, check the ferry times—and realize that the route matters just as much as the places you choose.

Our Greece travel packages are built around that reality. They connect Athens with the Greek islands and selected mainland destinations using ferries, domestic flights, and pre-arranged transfers where needed. Routes range from shorter cultural trips to longer journeys through Santorini, Mykonos, Crete, Rhodes, Naxos, Paros, Kefalonia, Zakynthos, Delphi, and Meteora.

Depending on the package, arrangements can include hotels with breakfast, guided sightseeing, entrance fees, airport and port transfers, ferries, domestic flights, and other transportation listed in the itinerary.
These are multi-day Greece vacations rather than cruise programs or fixed escorted circuits, giving you more freedom over where you go and how long you stay.

sections.heading: Start with the Route, Not the Island List

blocks.text: Greece looks compact on a map. Travelling between its islands tells a different story.

Two islands that appear close together may not have a convenient direct ferry on your travel date. Another combination may work beautifully because the islands sit on the same ferry route. Sometimes flying back through Athens is faster than trying to connect two islands by sea.
That is why adding another island does not always improve the trip.

For many first-time visitors, Athens, Mykonos, and Santorini work well together because the route is established and connections are relatively straightforward during the main season. Once you move beyond that combination, checking how the islands connect becomes increasingly important.

sections.heading: Which Part of Greece Do You Want to See?

blocks.text: Not every Greece vacation needs to follow the same island trail.
Santorini and Mykonos give you the familiar Cycladic combination: whitewashed villages, Aegean views, beaches, and two islands with very different personalities.
Naxos and Paros keep you in the Cyclades but offer another pace. They can make sense for travelers who want island time without building the entire trip around Greece's two most famous names.

Crete deserves to be treated differently. It is Greece's largest island and can easily take several days on its own, particularly if you want to combine towns, archaeological sites, beaches, and the interior.
Rhodes brings medieval history into an island itinerary, while Kefalonia and Zakynthos take you away from the Aegean altogether and into the Ionian Sea.
Choosing between them is less about which island is “best” and more about what kind of Greece trip you want.
It is easy to think of Greece as Athens plus the islands, but some routes are better with less time at sea.

Delphi can be incorporated into a cultural journey from Athens, while Meteora takes you north to one of the country's most distinctive landscapes, where monasteries sit above dramatic rock formations.
Adding mainland Greece can work particularly well when history is a major reason for your trip and you do not want every destination after Athens to be another island.
It also gives you more options outside the peak island season.

sections.heading: How Many Islands Is Too Many?

blocks.text: Hotel changes take time. So do ferry ports.

On travel days, you need to check out, reach the port, board the ferry, travel, disembark, transfer to the next hotel, and check in again. Even a relatively short ferry crossing can therefore use a meaningful part of the day.
For a one-week trip, two islands after Athens will often feel better than trying to squeeze in three. With more time, another island becomes practical—but only if the connections work.
Look at the number of nights, not simply the number of days printed in the tour title.
Two nights usually means only one full day between arrival and departure. Three nights gives you two.
That small difference can completely change how an island stay feels.
There is no rule that says a Greek island vacation has to be done entirely by ferry.

Ferries are part of the experience and work particularly well between islands with convenient direct connections. Domestic flights can save valuable time on longer routes or when an island does not connect efficiently with your next stop.
Some itineraries use both.
The better option depends on the islands, season, schedules, and how much of your vacation you are willing to spend in transit.
Quite a lot once islands are involved.

Late spring through early autumn offers the widest range of island services and ferry connections. July and August bring the busiest atmosphere, warmest weather, and strongest demand for hotels and transportation.
May, June, September, and early October can be particularly attractive when you want island time alongside comfortable sightseeing in Athens and mainland Greece.

Outside the main season, some ferry routes operate less frequently. Rather than choosing the islands first and checking transportation later, it is better to make sure the route works for your actual travel dates.
They are different ways of travelling through Greece.
Choose a Greece travel package when you want a multi-day itinerary with hotels and transportation arranged while keeping more independence between scheduled services.
A Greece Cruise Package makes more sense when you prefer to travel between destinations by ship and return to the same accommodation each night.
For travelers who prefer a fixed program with more of the journey organized around scheduled group sightseeing, our Greece Escorted Tours offer another approach.
For the complete collection of destinations and travel styles, browse our Greece Tours.

faqs.q: What do Greece travel packages typically include?
faqs.a: Standard packages include: a licensed English-speaking guide for all site visits, 3 to 4-star hotels in Athens (near the Plaka) and boutique cliff-side hotels in Santorini (Oia or Fira), daily breakfast, private vehicle transfers in Athens, ferry or flight connections between islands, and entrance fees to all listed sites including the Acropolis. The licensed archaeologist guide for the Acropolis is required by Greek law and is included.

faqs.q: How many days are recommended for a Greece trip?
faqs.a: Eight days covers Athens and two Cyclades islands (typically Santorini and Mykonos) at a comfortable pace. Five days suits Athens with a Santorini extension. Twelve days allows the islands plus the Classical mainland circuit (Delphi, Meteora). Most first-time visitors find 8 days the right balance between the city and the islands.

faqs.q: Do Greece travel packages include island hopping?
faqs.a: Yes. Island connections by high-speed ferry or short-haul domestic flight are included in packages covering multiple islands. The Athens to Santorini connection is typically a 2-hour domestic flight or a 7-hour high-speed ferry. The Santorini to Mykonos connection is a 2-hour ferry. All ferry and flight bookings are arranged and included in the package price.

faqs.q: How much does a Greece travel package cost in 2026?
faqs.a: Five-day Athens-only packages cost approximately 900 to 1,400 USD per person based on double occupancy. Eight-day Athens, Santorini, and Mykonos packages cost approximately 1,800 to 2,800 USD per person, depending on hotel category, season, and group size. Small group departures are typically 25 to 35 percent less per person.

faqs.q: Is a licensed guide included for the Acropolis?
faqs.a: Yes. Greek law (Law 710/1977) requires a licensed guide for all groups at archaeological sites in Greece. A licensed archaeologist guide is included in all Magnificent Travel Greece packages for the Acropolis visit. The standard Acropolis program covers the Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaea, and Temple of Athena Nike over approximately 2 to 3 hours.

faqs.q: What is included in a Santorini package?
faqs.a: Standard Santorini programs include: 2 to 3 nights in a boutique cliff-side hotel in Oia or Fira (caldera-view rooms), a caldera boat cruise (visiting the volcanic islet of Nea Kameni, the hot springs, and the pumice beach), and a guided visit to the Akrotiri Bronze Age excavation site. Oia village sunset viewing is the most popular evening activity and requires no guide.

faqs.q: Can I book a private Greece tour for a family with children?
faqs.a: Yes. Private tours are available for families with children of any age. The Acropolis is fully accessible by paved path (no steps required). Santorini's Akrotiri is a covered excavation site, suitable for all ages. The caldera boat cruise takes approximately 3 hours and is calm-water sailing in the caldera bay. Mykonos has a beach club culture that works for all ages.

faqs.q: What is the best base for exploring Athens?
faqs.a: The Plaka neighbourhood at the base of the Acropolis hill is the standard base for Athens programs. Hotels here are within 10 minutes' walk of the Acropolis entrance. Syntagma Square is 15 minutes on foot and provides access to the Parliament building, the National Garden, and the metro system. Magnificent Travel uses hotels in the Plaka or Monastiraki areas by default.

faqs.q: Can I add Crete to a Greece travel package?
faqs.a: Yes. Crete can be added after Santorini or Mykonos on packages of 10 days or more. A 3-night Crete program covers Knossos Palace (the Minoan palace complex, 1700 BC, the largest Bronze Age site in the Aegean), Heraklion Archaeological Museum (Minoan artefacts including the Phaistos Disc), and the Samaria Gorge (18 km, a full-day walk). The ferry from Santorini to Crete takes approximately 2 hours.

faqs.q: Is Delphi included in Greece travel packages?
faqs.a: Delphi is not included in standard island-focused packages. It is included in mainland Greece escorted tours and can be added as a day trip from Athens (3 hours by road) on extended programs. See Greece escorted tours for programs that include Delphi, Meteora, and Olympia, or day tours in Greece for the Delphi day excursion.
